claims.text: Controlled annealing will produce a nonmonotonic change in the critical temperature of the target high-entropy alloy superconductor.
An intermediate degree of lattice disorder will maximize Tc relative to the as-cast state.
The starting material is an as-cast, single-phase, disordered high-entropy alloy superconductor.
The target alloy contains at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
The target alloy is outside Nb-Ta-based and Ti-rich systems.
Varying annealing temperature and duration can progressively reduce lattice disorder and promote short-range chemical order without inducing phase separation.
The relevant superconducting measurements are typically performed below 10 K.
A random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii produces severe lattice distortion and variations in interatomic distance in HEAs.
Annealing changes the target alloy's local atomic environment by changing lattice disorder and short-range chemical order.
Annealing-induced changes in the local atomic environment alter the electronic density of states and inter-element interactions.
Intermediate lattice disorder enhances Cooper-pair formation.
Both the highly disordered as-cast state and an overly ordered state have less favorable superconducting pairing conditions than an intermediately disordered state.
Tc will first rise above the as-cast baseline and then fall under more extensive annealing because of excessive ordering.
The as-cast baseline has a maximally disordered atomic configuration.
The proposed relationship applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase disordered solid solution without secondary phases.
Composition and phase purity can affect structural ordering or decomposition in HEAs.
The optimal annealing temperature, duration, and magnitude of the Tc change depend on elemental makeup and local chemical interactions.
Resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility measurements can be used together to identify and confirm Tc.
Failure to observe a statistically significant intermediate Tc maximum relative to the as-cast control would falsify the proposed nonmonotonic-disorder hypothesis.
